mechanism.identifier: Apple Account: Password & Security > Security Keys enrollment

description_intent: Whether an Apple Account is protected by a hardware security key is a binary fact about that account, not a device setting a management profile can push: either one or more physical tokens have been registered against the account as an authentication factor, or none have. Nothing about this state lives in a plist key or a settings-catalog policy - it is read back by opening the account's own security settings and looking at what is listed there, which is why the check is a manual look rather than a scripted one. The benchmark leaves the enrollment decision itself to the organization's own requirements, with an explicit allowance for legacy or test devices that can't meet it; this spec records enrollment (true) as the hardening direction the control's own rationale points toward.
rationale_intent: A password and a one-time code both travel as data a person can be tricked into typing into the wrong place - a convincing login page captures either one exactly as easily as the real service would have accepted it. A hardware security key does not work that way: it answers a cryptographic challenge tied to the specific origin asking for it, so a copy of that exchange handed to a lookalike site simply does not verify anywhere else, and there is no code or string for a person to be talked into repeating. Registering a key against an Apple Account replaces a factor that can be captured and reused with one that only ever proves itself to the genuine service - that substitution, not merely the addition of a second factor, is the actual gap this control closes.
